questions.question: How does a Helm chart work — its structure, values, and templating model?
questions.title: Helm Charts: Structure, Values Overrides, and Go Templating
questions.direct_answer: A Helm chart is a directory with `Chart.yaml` (metadata), `values.yaml` (default config), a `templates/` folder (Go-templated Kubernetes manifests), and optional `charts/` for dependencies. `helm install` renders templates with values (built-in `.Chart`, `.Release`, plus user `.Values`) into real manifests and applies them. Multi-environment setups use `-f values-prod.yaml` override files and `--set` flags. Templates use Go template syntax (`{{ .Values.image.tag }}`), Sprig functions (`toYaml`, `required`), named templates (`{{- define }}`), and helpers in `_helpers.tpl`. `helm lint` + `helm template --debug` validate before install.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Helm as a template + release manager, not just a CLI
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating `values.yaml` as environment-specific config (hardcoding prod values there) instead of keeping it as the chart's defaults and layering env-specific override files
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain `_helpers.tpl`, named templates, `required` / `default` Sprig functions, `lookup` for cross-resource refs, subchart value overrides, `helm template --debug`, and the split between chart defaults vs env overrides

sections.title: Why Helm Exists: Raw YAML Doesn't Scale Across Environments
sections.content:
A microservice deployed to dev, staging, and prod has the same shape but different values: replicas, image tag, resource sizes, ingress host, secret references. Maintaining three copies of the same 800-line YAML diverges quickly — someone fixes a bug in prod but forgets staging. **Kustomize** answers this with patch overlays. **Helm** answers with **templated charts** plus **release management** (install, upgrade, rollback, history, hooks).

A Helm chart has four critical pieces:

- **`Chart.yaml`** — metadata: name, version (chart SemVer), `appVersion` (the app's SemVer), optional `dependencies`.
- **`values.yaml`** — **default** config for the chart. Not environment-specific — think "what a fresh install would use."
- **`templates/`** — Go-templated Kubernetes manifests. Each file becomes rendered manifests at `helm install` time.
- **`charts/`** — optional subcharts (dependencies) like a bundled Redis or ingress.

The rendering model: `helm install my-release ./mychart -f values-prod.yaml --set image.tag=1.2.3` merges values in priority order (CLI `--set` > `-f` files > chart `values.yaml`), injects built-ins (`.Release.Name`, `.Chart.Version`, `.Files`), and renders the templates into plain Kubernetes YAML. Helm then applies the rendered manifests to the cluster and records the release in a Kubernetes Secret (the **release record**).

sections.title: From Chart + Values to Deployed Release
sections.content:
Templates + merged values → rendered manifests → applied to cluster → release record stored as a Secret.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Chart[Chart.yaml\nversion, appVersion]
    ValsDefault[values.yaml\nchart defaults]
    ValsEnv[values-prod.yaml\nenv overrides]
    CLISet[--set image.tag=1.2.3]
    Tmpl[templates/\n*.yaml with Go template]
    Helpers[_helpers.tpl\nnamed templates]
    Engine[Helm Render\nGo template + Sprig]
    Rendered[Rendered manifests\nDeployment, Service, etc]
    K8s[Kubernetes API]
    Release[Release Secret\nhistory + rollback data]

    Chart --> Engine
    ValsDefault --> Engine
    ValsEnv --> Engine
    CLISet --> Engine
    Tmpl --> Engine
    Helpers --> Engine
    Engine --> Rendered
    Rendered --> K8s
    Engine -.records.-> Release
    Release -. helm history / rollback .-> Engine
```

Every `helm install` or `upgrade` stores a release record so `helm history` and `helm rollback` work without external state.

sections.title: Chart Anatomy: A Realistic `templates/deployment.yaml`
Multi-Environment Pattern: Chart Defaults + Env Overrides
sections.content:
The common mistake: putting prod-specific values directly into `values.yaml`. The correct pattern keeps `values.yaml` as minimal defaults, then layers environment override files.

```
mychart/
├─ Chart.yaml
├─ values.yaml             # chart defaults (replicas: 1, resources: small)
├─ templates/
env/
├─ values-dev.yaml        # dev overrides
├─ values-staging.yaml
└─ values-prod.yaml       # replicas: 6, HPA enabled, prod ingress host
```

Install per environment:

```bash
helm upgrade --install order-service ./mychart \
  --namespace prod --create-namespace \
  -f env/values-prod.yaml \
  --set image.tag=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD) \
  --atomic --timeout 5m
```

**Key flags:**

- `--install` — idempotent (install if not present, upgrade if present). The bedrock of GitOps-friendly Helm.
- `--atomic` — if the upgrade fails, roll back to the previous release. Never leaves the cluster in a half-applied state.
- `--timeout 5m` — wait up to 5 min for resources to reach Ready. Essential with readiness probes.
- `--dry-run` + `helm template` — inspect rendered YAML without applying.

**Validation workflow:**

```bash
helm lint ./mychart -f env/values-prod.yaml
helm template my-release ./mychart -f env/values-prod.yaml --debug > rendered.yaml
kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f rendered.yaml    # server-side validation
```

Run this in CI as a gate. `helm template --debug` shows which values came from which source — invaluable when overrides don't take effect.

sections.title: Subcharts, Library Charts, and Common Helm Pitfalls
sections.content:
**Subcharts (dependencies).** Declare in `Chart.yaml`:

```yaml
dependencies:
  - name: postgresql
    version: 12.5.8
    repository: https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
    condition: postgresql.enabled
```

Run `helm dependency update` to pull into `charts/`. Override subchart values by nesting:

```yaml
# parent values.yaml
postgresql:
  enabled: true
  auth:
    postgresPassword: changeme
```

**Global values.** `global.X` in the parent values is visible to all subcharts — useful for shared image registry, labels, environment.

**Library charts.** A library chart (`type: library` in Chart.yaml) has no templates of its own — it exports reusable helpers via `_helpers.tpl` for consumption by application charts. Pattern: centralize labels, probes, securityContext defaults.

**Common pitfalls:**

- **Whitespace / indentation bugs** — use `nindent N` consistently; `helm template --debug` reveals rendering problems.
- **`toYaml` on nil** — if `.Values.resources` is unset, `toYaml` emits `null`. Guard with `{{- with .Values.resources }}{{- toYaml . | nindent 12 }}{{- end }}`.
- **Trusting `appVersion` for image tag** — `appVersion` is a string in `Chart.yaml`, not synced with CI. Most teams pass `image.tag` via `--set` from CI.
- **Hardcoding namespace inside templates** — use `{{ .Release.Namespace }}` so a single chart deploys to different namespaces per environment.
- **Missing `resources.requests`** — chart defaults with empty resources trip up HPA downstream; set sensible defaults in `values.yaml`.
- **Not using `--atomic`** — failed upgrades leave a half-applied state; always use `--atomic --timeout` in CI.
- **Secret handling** — do NOT commit secrets to `values-prod.yaml`; use `--set` from CI secrets, SOPS-encrypted values, Sealed Secrets, or External Secrets Operator.

**`helm diff` plugin.** `helm diff upgrade my-release ./mychart -f values-prod.yaml` shows exactly what would change — production review should require a diff before every upgrade.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Four pieces: `Chart.yaml`, `values.yaml`, `templates/`, optional `charts/`** — metadata, defaults, Go-templated manifests, subcharts.
- **Values merge priority: `--set` > `-f files` > chart defaults** — CLI wins, enabling per-environment composition.
- **`_helpers.tpl` hosts named templates** — `include` them for labels, names, selectors; library charts share helpers across many app charts.
- **Keep `values.yaml` as chart defaults, not env config** — env-specific values live in `values-prod.yaml` etc; chart remains reusable.
- **Use `--atomic --timeout`** — failed upgrades roll back automatically; never leaves half-applied state.
- **`helm template --debug` is the primary debugging tool** — reveals which value came from which source and how whitespace rendered.
- **Secrets do NOT belong in `values-prod.yaml`** — use `--set` from CI secrets, SOPS, Sealed Secrets, or External Secrets Operator.
- **Subcharts inherit `global.*` values** — centralize image registry, labels, environment flags in the parent chart.
- **Release record is a Kubernetes Secret** — `helm history` and `helm rollback` work without external state.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A Helm chart is a directory with four important pieces: `Chart.yaml` for metadata, `values.yaml` for chart defaults, a `templates/` folder with Go-templated Kubernetes manifests, and an optional `charts/` folder for dependencies.

**How rendering works**
- `helm install` merges values in priority order — CLI `--set` wins, then `-f` override files, then the chart's own `values.yaml`.
- Helm injects built-in values like `.Release.Name`, `.Release.Namespace`, `.Chart.Name`, and `.Chart.AppVersion` alongside the user values.
- The Go template engine plus Sprig functions renders the manifests; Helm then applies them and stores a release record as a Kubernetes Secret, which is what `helm history` and `helm rollback` use.

**Multi-environment pattern**
- Keep `values.yaml` as minimal chart defaults — what a fresh install would use.
- Environment-specific overrides live in separate files like `values-prod.yaml` with prod replica count, resource sizes, ingress host.
- CI installs with `helm upgrade --install --atomic --timeout 5m -f values-prod.yaml --set image.tag=$GIT_SHA`.
- `--atomic` is the most important flag — if the upgrade fails, Helm rolls back automatically, so the cluster is never in a half-applied state.

**Helpers and reuse**
- `_helpers.tpl` defines named templates for labels, names, selectors; you `include` them inside other templates.
- Library charts (`type: library`) export helpers without any templates of their own — good pattern for centralizing probes, securityContext, labels across many app charts.
- `required "error message" .Values.image.repository` fails render with a clear message when a mandatory value is missing.

**Debugging and validation**
- `helm lint` catches basic chart issues; run in CI.
- `helm template --debug` shows which value came from which source and reveals whitespace rendering bugs — the #1 Helm frustration.
- `helm diff upgrade` plugin shows exactly what would change vs the current release — production PR review should require a diff.

**Secrets and security**
- Don't commit secrets into `values-prod.yaml` — use `--set` from CI secret stores, SOPS-encrypted values, Sealed Secrets, or External Secrets Operator.
- Subcharts inherit `global.*` values — centralize image registry, environment labels, and shared config at the parent level.

questions.question: How does Helm manage release lifecycle — install, upgrade, rollback, and history?
questions.title: Helm Release Lifecycle: Install, Upgrade, Rollback, History
questions.direct_answer: Helm tracks each deployment as a **release** — a versioned record stored as a Kubernetes Secret in the target namespace. `helm upgrade --install` is idempotent (installs if absent, upgrades if present). `--atomic` rolls back on failure. `helm history` lists all revisions; `helm rollback REVISION` reverts to a previous version including all manifests. Hooks (pre-install, post-upgrade) run ordered Jobs for DB migrations. `helm get manifest/values/hooks` retrieves exactly what was applied. This is why Helm beats raw `kubectl apply` — the release record enables safe, audited rollback.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand Helm as a release manager with history, not just a templating tool
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Running `helm install` twice (errors on existing release) instead of `helm upgrade --install`, or skipping `--atomic` so failed upgrades leave a half-applied state
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain hooks and weights, how rollback reverts all manifests not just image, the 3-way merge patch, `revisionHistoryLimit`, secret-based state, Helm 3 removal of Tiller, and how GitOps tools layer on top

sections.title: The Release Record: What `helm install` Actually Creates
sections.content:
`kubectl apply` has no memory. If you apply a manifest and it breaks production, your only recovery is `git revert` plus re-apply — hoping the state in git matches what was actually applied. **Helm fixes this** by treating every `install` or `upgrade` as a versioned **release** — a record stored as a Kubernetes Secret (type `helm.sh/release.v1`) in the release's namespace, containing:

- The full rendered manifests as applied.
- The merged values used.
- The chart metadata (name, version).
- Hooks that ran.
- Status (deployed, failed, pending-upgrade, superseded).

Every upgrade creates a new revision; old revisions are retained up to `revisionHistoryLimit` (default 10). This is what enables `helm history`, `helm rollback`, and `helm get manifest` — **the cluster itself stores the release state**. No external DB, no Tiller (removed in Helm 3), just Secrets in the namespace.

This is the foundation for safe production operations: you can see exactly what was deployed at any revision, diff it against the current state, and roll back to any prior revision with a single command.

sections.title: Release Lifecycle: From Install Through Failed Upgrade and Rollback
sections.content:
Each operation creates a new revision; `--atomic` auto-rolls back on failure.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Dev as Developer/CI
    participant Helm as Helm Client
    participant K8s as Kubernetes API
    participant Sec as Release Secret

    Dev->>Helm: helm install order-svc ./chart -f prod.yaml
    Helm->>Helm: render templates + values
    Helm->>K8s: apply Deployment/Service/Ingress
    Helm->>Sec: store revision 1 (deployed)
    Note over Dev,Sec: Later...
    Dev->>Helm: helm upgrade --install --atomic --set image.tag=1.2
    Helm->>Sec: create revision 2 (pending-upgrade)
    Helm->>K8s: apply new manifests
    Helm->>K8s: wait for readiness (--timeout)
    K8s-->>Helm: rollout failed
    Helm->>Helm: --atomic triggered
    Helm->>K8s: rollback to revision 1 manifests
    Helm->>Sec: revision 2 marked failed, revision 3 deployed = copy of 1
    Dev->>Helm: helm history order-svc
    Helm->>Sec: list all revisions
    Dev->>Helm: helm rollback order-svc 1
    Helm->>K8s: apply revision 1 manifests
    Helm->>Sec: revision 4 deployed = copy of 1
```

Rollback creates a NEW revision that mirrors the target — history is append-only; you never lose the failed revision.

sections.title: The Idempotent Deploy: `helm upgrade --install --atomic`
sections.content:
CI pipelines should call exactly one Helm command for both first-time install and subsequent upgrades:

```bash
helm upgrade --install order-svc ./chart \
  --namespace prod --create-namespace \
  -f env/values-prod.yaml \
  --set image.tag=${GIT_SHA} \
  --atomic \
  --timeout 5m \
  --wait
```

**What each flag does:**

- **`--install`** — if release doesn't exist, install; if it does, upgrade. Idempotent.
- **`--atomic`** — if apply or readiness wait fails, roll back to previous revision. **Never** leaves a half-applied state.
- **`--timeout 5m`** — wait up to 5 minutes for resources to reach Ready. Gives readiness probes room.
- **`--wait`** — wait for all resources (including Deployments, StatefulSets, Jobs) to be Ready before marking deployed.
- **`--create-namespace`** — create the namespace if absent.

**Inspecting what happened:**

```bash
helm history order-svc -n prod
# REVISION  UPDATED                  STATUS       CHART         APP VERSION  DESCRIPTION
# 1         2026-04-10 14:32:11 UTC  superseded   order-1.0.0   1.2.0        Install complete
# 2         2026-04-12 09:15:43 UTC  failed       order-1.0.0   1.2.1        Upgrade "order-svc" failed
# 3         2026-04-12 09:16:12 UTC  deployed     order-1.0.0   1.2.0        Rollback to 1

helm get values order-svc -n prod             # current values
helm get manifest order-svc -n prod            # exact rendered manifests
helm get manifest order-svc --revision 1       # revision 1 specifically
helm diff upgrade order-svc ./chart -f prod.yaml   # (plugin) preview upgrade
```

`helm get manifest --revision N` is the source of truth for "what was running at revision N" — use it in incident reviews and audits.

sections.title: Hooks for Migrations and Ordering: Pre-Install, Post-Upgrade, Weights
sections.content:
Hooks are Kubernetes manifests annotated with `helm.sh/hook` — they run at specific lifecycle points as ordered Jobs.

```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: db-migrate-{{ .Release.Revision }}
  annotations:
    helm.sh/hook: pre-upgrade,pre-install
    helm.sh/hook-weight: "0"
    helm.sh/hook-delete-policy: before-hook-creation,hook-succeeded
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: migrate
          image: flyway/flyway:latest
          args: ["migrate"]
      restartPolicy: Never
```

**Hook points** (common): `pre-install`, `post-install`, `pre-upgrade`, `post-upgrade`, `pre-delete`, `post-delete`, `pre-rollback`, `post-rollback`, `test`.

**Weight** (`hook-weight`) — hooks run in weight order, low first. Use for dependencies: DB migration (weight 0) before seed data (weight 10).

**Delete policy:**
- `before-hook-creation` — delete previous hook Job before creating new one.
- `hook-succeeded` — delete Job after success (keep if failed for debugging).
- `hook-failed` — delete if failed.

**Critical caveat:** Hook resources are NOT managed by regular Helm release tracking — they are not deleted on `helm uninstall` by default (unless the delete policy says so). They also do NOT participate in `helm rollback` — if a migration ran forward in revision 2 and you rollback to revision 1, the migration does not reverse automatically. Plan migrations as forward-compatible (add column before using it, drop only after no code references it).

**`helm test` — post-deploy smoke tests.** A Pod annotated `helm.sh/hook: test` runs with `helm test <release>` — basic health check after deploy. Common use: curl the liveness probe, run a minimal integration test.

sections.title: Rollback Semantics, 3-Way Merge, and GitOps Interaction
sections.content:
**What rollback actually does.**

```bash
helm rollback order-svc 1 -n prod          # go back to revision 1
```

Helm re-applies the manifests as they were at revision 1. New revision (e.g., 4) is created marked `deployed`, the rollback-from revision is marked `superseded`. **All manifests revert** — Deployment image, Service spec, Ingress rules, ConfigMap data. What is NOT reverted: hook side-effects (DB migrations already ran), Persistent data, external resources not managed by this chart.

**3-way merge patches.** Helm upgrade uses a 3-way merge: previous chart manifests + new chart manifests + live cluster state. This lets manual `kubectl edit` survive upgrades for fields Helm didn't manage — but also means manual edits to Helm-managed fields silently disappear on next upgrade. Rule: **don't kubectl-edit Helm-managed resources**; change the chart and upgrade.

**`revisionHistoryLimit`** — default 10 revisions kept. Raise for frequent-deploy services to give longer rollback window; lower to reduce Secret clutter in the namespace.

**Secret-based state considerations:**

- Release secrets are stored in the release namespace — so RBAC on Secrets governs who can see release history.
- Large charts can exceed the Secret size limit (~1MB encoded). For very large charts, switch storage to ConfigMap or split the chart.
- Release name must be unique in the namespace. `helm list -A` to find existing releases.

**GitOps tools (ArgoCD, Flux) vs Helm CLI.**

- ArgoCD can deploy Helm charts without calling `helm install` — it renders via `helm template` and applies with its own controller. The "release" then lives in ArgoCD's Application resource, not as a Helm Secret; `helm history` is empty.
- Flux Helm Controller uses real Helm releases, preserving `helm history` and rollback.
- Trade-off: ArgoCD's approach avoids dual ownership (ArgoCD vs Helm) but loses `helm rollback`; you roll back by reverting Git.
- For strict GitOps, Git is the source of truth — manual `helm rollback` diverges from Git and ArgoCD will revert it. In GitOps-only shops, rollback = Git revert.

**Failure modes and recovery:**

- **Stuck `pending-upgrade` release.** Helm thinks an upgrade is in progress but the process died. `helm rollback <release> <prev-rev>` usually clears it; or `helm history` + manual Secret cleanup.
- **`failed` release blocks future upgrades.** Use `helm upgrade --force` or rollback first, then upgrade.
- **CRDs are not managed by `helm rollback`.** CRDs in `crds/` folder are install-only; upgrades don't touch them. Use OCI charts or external tooling for CRD lifecycle.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **A release is a Kubernetes Secret** (or ConfigMap) storing rendered manifests, values, and status — the cluster itself holds the release state; no external DB, no Tiller.
- **`helm upgrade --install --atomic --timeout` is the CI default** — idempotent, auto-rollback on failure, waits for readiness.
- **Every operation creates a revision** — `helm history` lists all; `helm rollback N` reverts to any prior; history is append-only.
- **Rollback re-applies all manifests** — Deployment image, Service, Ingress, ConfigMaps; does NOT reverse hook side-effects or external data.
- **Hooks run ordered Jobs by weight** — pre-install migrations, post-install seeds, post-upgrade smoke tests; design for forward-compat because rollback won't reverse them.
- **3-way merge preserves manual edits for fields Helm didn't set** — but Helm-managed fields revert on upgrade; don't kubectl-edit Helm resources.
- **`revisionHistoryLimit` controls rollback window** — default 10; tune for deploy frequency.
- **ArgoCD `helm template` mode loses `helm rollback`** — rollback = Git revert in GitOps-only shops; Flux Helm Controller preserves native Helm history.
- **CRDs in `crds/` are install-only** — not upgraded, not rolled back; manage separately.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Helm is more than a templating tool — it's a release manager. Every `helm install` or `upgrade` creates a release record stored as a Kubernetes Secret in the target namespace, containing the rendered manifests, the merged values, and the status. This record is what makes `helm history`, `helm rollback`, and `helm get manifest` work without any external database.

**The CI pattern**
- `helm upgrade --install order-svc ./chart -f values-prod.yaml --set image.tag=$SHA --atomic --timeout 5m --wait`.
- `--install` makes it idempotent — install if absent, upgrade if present — safe to run every deploy.
- `--atomic` is the most important flag — if apply or readiness wait fails, Helm rolls back to the previous revision; the cluster is never in a half-applied state.
- `--wait` blocks until all resources are Ready; `--timeout 5m` sets the ceiling.

**History and rollback**
- `helm history order-svc` lists every revision with status: deployed, superseded, failed.
- `helm rollback order-svc 3` reverts to revision 3 — re-applies the Deployment, Service, ConfigMap as they were at that revision. Creates a new revision (e.g., 7) that mirrors 3.
- `helm get manifest order-svc --revision 3` shows exactly what was applied at that point — essential for incident reviews.
- What rollback does NOT do: reverse hook side-effects (DB migrations) or restore external data. Design migrations to be forward-compatible so a rollback of manifests doesn't leave DB schema orphaned.

**Hooks for migrations**
- Jobs annotated `helm.sh/hook: pre-upgrade` run before the new manifests apply; use for DB migrations.
- `helm.sh/hook-weight` orders hooks; low runs first.
- `helm.sh/hook-delete-policy: before-hook-creation,hook-succeeded` cleans up Job history.
- `helm test` runs test-annotated pods post-deploy for smoke tests.

**Why Helm beats raw kubectl apply**
- kubectl apply has no history — you rely on Git to know what was applied, and nothing prevents drift between Git and cluster.
- Helm stores the actual applied manifests per revision, so rollback works even if Git is gone.
- `--atomic` gives safe failure handling that raw apply cannot match.

**Interaction with GitOps**
- ArgoCD can deploy Helm charts but often uses `helm template` mode — it renders and applies itself, so `helm history` is empty; rollback = Git revert.
- Flux Helm Controller uses real Helm releases — native `helm history` and rollback are preserved.
- In strict GitOps shops Git is the source of truth — manual `helm rollback` diverges and gets reverted by the GitOps controller.

**Common gotchas**
- CRDs in the `crds/` folder are install-only — upgrades don't touch them and rollback doesn't revert them.
- Don't kubectl-edit Helm-managed resources — your edits vanish on next upgrade because of 3-way merge.
- `revisionHistoryLimit` caps retained revisions; raise for frequent-deploy services to have a longer rollback window.

questions.question: Helm vs Kustomize: which one should you use for Kubernetes application packaging?
questions.title: Helm vs Kustomize: When to Use Each (and When to Combine)
questions.direct_answer: **Helm** is a templating + release manager — Go templates with values, subcharts for dependencies, built-in install/upgrade/rollback with revision history. Best for **third-party distribution** (you publish a chart others install) and when you need hooks for migrations. **Kustomize** is a patch-overlay tool — pure YAML with strategic merge and JSON patches, no templating, built into `kubectl`. Best for **internal apps with environment overlays** where templating feels heavy and you want the YAML to stay readable. In practice many teams **combine**: Helm for packaged apps (ingress-nginx, cert-manager, monitoring) + Kustomize for their own microservices.

interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain overlay vs template model, release management difference, combining Helm for 3rd-party + Kustomize for in-house, the Helm chart post-render with Kustomize pattern, and GitOps tool preferences

sections.title: Two Philosophies: Templating vs Overlay
sections.content:
Helm and Kustomize solve the same problem — configuring the same app for dev, staging, and prod — with fundamentally different philosophies.

**Helm — templating.** A chart is a template with placeholders: `image: {{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}`. Environment files (`values-prod.yaml`) provide the placeholder values. The rendered output is driven by values. **Power:** flexible, values-driven; can express any customization. **Cost:** templates become a second language on top of YAML; whitespace bugs; `helm template --debug` becomes muscle memory.

**Kustomize — overlay.** A base is plain Kubernetes YAML. Overlays are plain YAML patches that layer on top: `kustomization.yaml` declares which resources to include and which patches to apply. **Power:** everything stays as valid Kubernetes YAML — your editor's YAML linter works; no templating language. **Cost:** more verbose for deeply varied environments; no dependency management; no native release tracking.

Both are first-class: `helm install` applies Helm; `kubectl apply -k ./overlays/prod` applies Kustomize. Both integrate with ArgoCD and Flux.

The honest answer is that **the two excel at different problems**. Mixed environments are common, and combining them is a legitimate pattern.

sections.title: Feature-by-Feature Comparison
sections.content:
| | Helm | Kustomize |
|---|---|---|
| Approach | Go templates + values | YAML patches + overlays |
| Language complexity | Learning curve: Go templates, Sprig, helpers | Minimal: pure YAML |
| Release tracking | `helm history`, `helm rollback` | None built-in; relies on Git + GitOps tool |
| Hooks | `pre-install`, `post-upgrade` Jobs | None; handle in CI or separate Job resources |
| Dependencies | Subcharts declared in `Chart.yaml` | `components` (1.19+) or `bases` referencing other kustomizations |
| Distribution | `helm push` to OCI registry; public charts at Artifact Hub | No standard packaging; share via Git repo |
| Installation command | `helm install/upgrade` | `kubectl apply -k` (built into kubectl) |
| CRD lifecycle | `crds/` folder (install-only) | Plain apply |
| Secrets handling | `--set` + SOPS/Sealed Secrets; values not encrypted by default | Plain YAML; needs SOPS/Sealed Secrets |
| Best for | Third-party distribution, apps with migrations | Internal microservices, environment overlays |
| GitOps integration | ArgoCD (`helm template` or `helm` mode), Flux Helm Controller | ArgoCD native, Flux Kustomize Controller |

**Templating strength.** Helm's `range`, `if`, `include` is powerful for conditional inclusion (e.g., enable HPA only if `hpa.enabled`). Kustomize achieves conditional inclusion via separate overlay bases or `components`.

**Readability.** A Kustomize overlay's `deployment-patch.yaml` reads like plain Kubernetes:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: {name: order-svc}
spec:
  replicas: 6
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: app
          resources:
            requests: {cpu: 500m, memory: 1Gi}
```

The Helm equivalent mixes Go templating with YAML in ways that fight your linter. For internal teams, many engineers prefer Kustomize's readability.

sections.title: The Decision Framework
sections.content:
**Use Helm when:**

- **You are distributing a reusable application** (third-party product, internal shared service). Users expect `helm install` with a values file.
- **Dependencies matter.** Your app bundles a Redis, Postgres, or a shared library of helpers — subcharts handle this cleanly.
- **Hooks are required** for DB migrations, post-install setup, smoke tests orchestrated by Helm lifecycle.
- **You need native release management.** `helm history`, `helm rollback`, `helm get manifest --revision N` for incident review.
- **Highly parameterized apps.** 50+ tunable values across deployments, ingress, HPA — values-driven beats patch-driven here.

**Use Kustomize when:**

- **Internal microservice with 3 environments** (dev/staging/prod) and simple overlays.
- **YAML must stay readable** to the team — your engineers aren't Helm experts.
- **Tight GitOps integration** with ArgoCD or Flux — both handle Kustomize natively without any CLI layer.
- **You're already using `kubectl apply -k`** — no extra tooling install.
- **Secret references via ConfigMapGenerator / SecretGenerator** — Kustomize's native generators are convenient for per-env data.

**Combine both when (very common in practice):**

- Third-party charts (ingress-nginx, cert-manager, prometheus-stack, external-secrets) via Helm — install from the chart authors' upstream.
- In-house microservices via Kustomize — your team owns readable, patch-based YAML.
- GitOps tool glues both: ArgoCD `Application` resources reference one set of Helm values and another set of Kustomize paths; same repository, consistent workflow.

**Post-renderer pattern.** `helm template | kustomize build` (or `--post-renderer`) lets you render a Helm chart and then apply a Kustomize patch on top. Useful when a third-party chart nearly fits but you need a one-line change the chart doesn't expose as a value — post-rendering lets you patch without forking.

sections.title: Pitfalls, GitOps Preferences, and Migration Paths
sections.content:
**Helm pitfalls:**

- **Whitespace bugs in templates.** `nindent` vs `indent`, trailing newlines — `helm template --debug` shows exactly what rendered.
- **Hidden upgrade risks from 3-way merge.** Manual `kubectl edit` to a Helm-managed field silently disappears on next upgrade.
- **CRD lifecycle confusion.** `crds/` folder is install-only; upgrades won't update CRDs. Manage CRDs separately (another Helm release, Operator, or Kustomize).
- **Secret rendering in values.** `--set password=...` ends up in `helm get values` output; use Sealed Secrets / SOPS / External Secrets instead.

**Kustomize pitfalls:**

- **No release history.** Rely on Git (`git revert`) and your GitOps controller for rollback — which is fine if GitOps is the discipline, painful if you mix manual operations.
- **Patch verbosity for deeply nested structures.** `strategicMergePatch` for list items by selector is finicky; `JsonPatch` is powerful but verbose.
- **`configMapGenerator` name suffix.** Kustomize appends a hash to generated ConfigMap names so pods restart on change — great feature, but surprising first time you see `config-abcde12345`.
- **No hooks.** Migration jobs need to be plain Kubernetes Jobs you order in CI, not hooked into an apply lifecycle.

**GitOps tool preferences:**

- **ArgoCD** — treats Helm and Kustomize as equals; Application spec has `source.helm.values` or `source.kustomize.*`. Tends toward **`helm template` mode** (no native Helm releases) to keep Git as sole truth.
- **Flux** — `HelmRelease` CR (real Helm releases, `helm history` preserved) + `Kustomization` CR (native Kustomize). Slightly richer Helm integration than ArgoCD.

**Migration paths.**

- **Helm → Kustomize.** `helm template my-release ./chart -f values-prod.yaml > base.yaml` gives you a starting base. Then craft overlay patches by hand. Viable for small charts; painful for large ones with many conditional includes.
- **Kustomize → Helm.** Identify parameters that vary across overlays — those become `.Values`. Move constant bases into `templates/`. More effort but valuable if you want to distribute or add hooks.

**Bottom line.** For a single-company internal microservice with straightforward environment variance, Kustomize is often simpler and more readable. For shared platform components, operators, or anything distributed outside your team, Helm's release management and distribution model pay for the templating complexity.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Helm is templating + release management; Kustomize is patch overlays** — different philosophies, both first-class.
- **Helm wins for distribution and hooks** — third-party charts, apps with migrations, built-in `helm rollback` with history.
- **Kustomize wins for internal readability** — plain YAML, no templating language, built into `kubectl`, native GitOps.
- **Combining both is common** — Helm for third-party (ingress-nginx, cert-manager), Kustomize for in-house microservices.
- **Post-renderer pattern** — `helm template | kustomize build` patches a third-party chart without forking when needed config isn't exposed.
- **ArgoCD supports both equally; Flux has richer Helm via HelmRelease** — GitOps integration isn't a reason to pick one over the other.
- **Kustomize has no hooks or release history** — rely on Git + GitOps for rollback; handle migrations as separate orchestrated Jobs.
- **Helm's 3-way merge silently reverts kubectl-edits** — don't mix manual edits and Helm management on the same resource.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Helm and Kustomize both solve the same problem — configuring an app across environments — but with completely different philosophies.

**Helm is templating plus release management**
- Go templates with values; `{{ .Values.image.tag }}` gets substituted at install time.
- Built-in install, upgrade, rollback, and history — release state stored as a Kubernetes Secret in the cluster.
- Subcharts for dependencies; hooks for migrations; OCI distribution for sharing.
- Cost: learning Go templates plus Sprig; whitespace bugs; templating language layered on YAML.

**Kustomize is pure YAML overlays**
- A base of plain Kubernetes YAML; overlays are YAML patches applied via `kustomization.yaml`.
- Built into kubectl — `kubectl apply -k ./overlays/prod`.
- No templating language — your YAML linter works; engineers read Kubernetes YAML directly.
- Cost: no release history, no hooks, more verbose for deeply varied configurations.

**When Helm wins**
- Distributing an application for others to install — third-party charts like ingress-nginx, cert-manager, prometheus-stack.
- Apps with DB migrations or setup Jobs — hooks orchestrate them in the lifecycle.
- Native rollback and history — `helm rollback` + `helm get manifest --revision N` for incident review.
- Heavily parameterized apps with 50+ tunable values — values-driven beats patch-driven.

**When Kustomize wins**
- Internal microservices with straightforward environment overlays.
- Teams that prefer readable YAML without a templating DSL.
- Tight ArgoCD or Flux GitOps where Git is the sole source of truth and rollback = Git revert.
- Already using `kubectl apply -k` — no extra tooling to install.

**The common pattern in practice**
- Most teams combine both: Helm for third-party components (the charts already exist and are well-tested), Kustomize for their own microservices.
- ArgoCD Application spec handles both seamlessly — one repository can contain Helm values and Kustomize overlays side by side.
- Post-renderer pattern — `helm template | kustomize build` — patches a third-party chart without forking when needed config isn't exposed as a value.

**Gotchas to call out**
- Helm's 3-way merge silently reverts kubectl edits to Helm-managed fields on the next upgrade — don't manually edit; change the chart.
- Kustomize's configMapGenerator appends a hash suffix to ConfigMap names — surprising at first but crucial for pod restart on config change.
- Helm CRDs in `crds/` are install-only — not upgraded; manage separately.
- In strict GitOps with ArgoCD in `helm template` mode, `helm history` is empty — rollback = Git revert, not `helm rollback`.

questions.question: What is GitOps and how do ArgoCD and Flux implement it for Kubernetes?
questions.title: GitOps with ArgoCD and Flux: Declarative Deployment and Drift Detection
questions.direct_answer: GitOps makes **Git the single source of truth** for desired cluster state. A controller in the cluster (ArgoCD or Flux) continuously pulls manifests from Git, applies them, and reconciles drift. Deployments become pull-requests, rollbacks become `git revert`, audit is automatic. **ArgoCD**: opinionated, strong UI, multi-cluster via `Application` / `ApplicationSet` CRDs, heavy on Helm / Kustomize rendering. **Flux**: modular (`source-controller`, `kustomize-controller`, `helm-controller`, `notification-controller`), preserves native Helm releases, tightly Kubernetes-native. Choose ArgoCD for UX + multi-team visibility; Flux for modular pipelines + stronger Helm parity.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of GitOps philosophy + practical differences between ArgoCD and Flux
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating GitOps as 'just auto-deploy from Git' instead of understanding drift reconciliation, declarative desired state, and the pull vs push distinction

sections.title: GitOps in One Sentence: Git Is the Desired State, a Controller Reconciles
sections.content:
Before GitOps, deployment was imperative: a CI job ran `kubectl apply` (or `helm upgrade`) against the cluster from outside. The cluster had no memory of desired state beyond what was last applied. **Drift** — when live state diverges from what was intended — went unnoticed until the next incident.

**GitOps inverts this.** The desired state of everything — Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, NetworkPolicies, CRDs — lives as YAML (or Helm/Kustomize) in a Git repository. A **controller inside the cluster** continuously:

1. Pulls the repository.
2. Compares desired (Git) vs live (cluster).
3. Reconciles differences — either applying Git to cluster (auto-sync) or alerting for manual approval.

Consequences:

- **Rollback = `git revert`**. The controller reconciles the old state back.
- **Audit = `git log`**. Every change is a signed commit or PR.
- **Drift detection is continuous.** Manual `kubectl edit` is noticed (and reverted, if auto-sync is on).
- **Pull-based, not push.** CI doesn't need cluster credentials; the cluster pulls from Git. Security win in regulated environments.

The two canonical implementations are **ArgoCD** (Intuit, now CNCF graduated) and **Flux** (Weaveworks, CNCF graduated). Both are production-grade; choice often comes down to UX preferences and Helm integration needs.

sections.title: Pull-Based Reconciliation Loop
sections.content:
CI builds images and updates Git; the in-cluster controller reconciles Git → cluster. CI never talks to the cluster directly.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Dev[Developer] -->|PR| GitApp[App Repo\nsource code]
    CI[CI: build + push] -->|new image tag| Registry[Container Registry]
    CI -->|commit: update image.tag\nin values.yaml| GitEnv[Env Repo\nK8s manifests]
    subgraph Cluster
        Ctrl[ArgoCD / Flux Controller]
        API[Kubernetes API]
        Apps[Deployments, Services\nConfigMaps, Ingress]
    end
    Ctrl -->|poll or webhook| GitEnv
    Ctrl -->|apply| API
    API --> Apps
    Ctrl -->|watch drift| API
    Ctrl -->|revert manual edits\nif auto-sync| API
    Ctrl -.notify.-> Slack[Slack / PagerDuty]
```

**Two-repo pattern** (common): app repo has source + Dockerfile; env repo has manifests. CI builds image, then commits updated `image.tag` to env repo. Controller picks up and deploys. This separates build-time concerns from deploy-time concerns cleanly.

**Single-repo pattern**: manifests and source in the same repo. Simpler for small teams; harder to give different RBAC to ops vs dev.

sections.title: ArgoCD: Application CRDs, UI, and Multi-Cluster Fan-Out
sections.content:
ArgoCD is installed into a management cluster. An **`Application`** CRD points at a Git path + destination cluster/namespace:

```yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata: {name: order-svc-prod, namespace: argocd}
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/org/platform-manifests
    path: apps/order-svc/overlays/prod
    targetRevision: HEAD
  destination:
    server: https://prod-cluster-api
    namespace: order-svc-prod
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true        # delete resources removed from Git
      selfHeal: true     # revert manual cluster edits
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=true
      - ServerSideApply=true
```

**ApplicationSet** (template for many Applications):

```yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: ApplicationSet
spec:
  generators:
    - list:
        elements:
          - {env: dev, cluster: dev-cluster}
          - {env: staging, cluster: stg-cluster}
          - {env: prod, cluster: prod-cluster}
  template:
    metadata: {name: 'order-svc-{{env}}'}
    spec:
      source:
        path: 'apps/order-svc/overlays/{{env}}'
      destination:
        server: '{{cluster}}'
```

One ApplicationSet manages a fleet — add a new environment, a new Application appears automatically.

**Strengths.** Rich UI showing sync status and manifests. Multi-cluster via destination servers. Strong RBAC (Projects isolate namespaces / repos / destinations). Progressive delivery via Argo Rollouts (canary, blue-green with analysis).

**Helm gotcha.** ArgoCD renders Helm charts with `helm template` by default — no native Helm release. `helm history` is empty; rollback = Git revert. For teams that want native `helm rollback`, use Flux or enable ArgoCD's Helm value Files via the Helm plugin (but most shops accept Git-first rollback).

sections.title: Flux: Modular Controllers, HelmRelease, and Image Automation
sections.content:
Flux is installed into the target cluster(s) via `flux bootstrap`. It is a set of focused controllers:

- **`source-controller`** — fetches Git / Helm repo / OCI artifact sources.
- **`kustomize-controller`** — reconciles Kustomize `Kustomization` resources.
- **`helm-controller`** — reconciles `HelmRelease` (real Helm releases, preserving `helm history`).
- **`notification-controller`** — Slack, GitHub status, webhooks.
- **`image-reflector-controller`** + **`image-automation-controller`** — watches registries and commits new tags back to Git automatically.

```yaml
apiVersion: source.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1
kind: GitRepository
metadata: {name: platform, namespace: flux-system}
spec:
  interval: 1m
  url: https://github.com/org/platform-manifests
  ref: {branch: main}
---
apiVersion: kustomize.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1
kind: Kustomization
spec:
  path: ./apps/order-svc/overlays/prod
  sourceRef: {kind: GitRepository, name: platform}
  prune: true
  interval: 2m
---
apiVersion: helm.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v2
kind: HelmRelease
spec:
  chart:
    spec: {chart: ./charts/order-svc, sourceRef: {kind: GitRepository, name: platform}}
  values:
    image: {tag: 1.2.3}
```

**Image automation.** Flux can watch a registry for new tags matching a regex and commit updates to Git automatically — closing the loop end-to-end without a separate CI job for the bump commit.

**Strengths.** Modular (use only the pieces you need). Native Helm releases (`helm history` works). First-class image automation. Lightweight — no UI (use Weave GitOps or the Flux Web UI as separate components).

**Weakness.** UI story is less polished than ArgoCD's out-of-the-box experience. Multi-cluster needs Flux installed per cluster with Git repo references — less centralized than ArgoCD's management-cluster model.

sections.title: Secrets, Progressive Delivery, and Choosing Between Them
sections.content:
**Secrets in GitOps.** Plain secrets in Git is a no-go. Three mainstream patterns:

- **Sealed Secrets (Bitnami).** Encrypt secrets into `SealedSecret` CR using cluster's public key; `kubeseal` CLI encrypts. Sealed Secret controller decrypts inside cluster.
- **SOPS (Mozilla).** Encrypts YAML files with KMS / age / gpg. Flux has native SOPS integration; ArgoCD uses a plugin or pre-render step.
- **External Secrets Operator (ESO).** Pulls secrets from AWS Secrets Manager / HashiCorp Vault / Azure Key Vault into Kubernetes Secrets. Nothing secret in Git; ESO references external store.

ESO is increasingly the default — secrets stay in a purpose-built vault, Kubernetes syncs them on demand. Rotation is handled by the vault.

**Progressive delivery.**

- **Argo Rollouts** (ArgoCD ecosystem) — CRD for canary and blue-green with automated analysis (Prometheus metric thresholds). Replaces the plain Deployment.
- **Flagger** (Flux ecosystem) — similar canary/blue-green, integrates with service mesh (Istio, Linkerd) for traffic weighting; works with plain Deployments.

**ArgoCD vs Flux decision:**

| Need | Lean |
|---|---|
| Rich UI for multi-team visibility | ArgoCD |
| Native Helm releases + `helm rollback` | Flux |
| Image tag automation from registry into Git | Flux |
| Progressive delivery with Prometheus analysis | Argo Rollouts (ArgoCD) or Flagger (Flux) |
| Multi-cluster fan-out from one control plane | ArgoCD (ApplicationSet) |
| Lightweight, per-cluster deployment | Flux |
| Windows / non-standard runtime support | ArgoCD |

**Common pitfalls:**

- **Auto-sync in prod without review.** Risk: a bad commit auto-deploys. Mitigation: protected branches + required PR reviews + `syncPolicy.automated.prune: true` only where safe.
- **Drift on CRDs.** Operators modify CRs at runtime (e.g., status fields). Mark those fields as `IgnoreDifferences` to avoid sync loops.
- **`prune` deleting resources you didn't expect.** An orphan ConfigMap from a previous manifest can be deleted; check before enabling.
- **Large repos = slow reconciliation.** Split into multiple Git sources or scope Applications by path.
- **RBAC on Git matters more than on kubectl.** Anyone who can push to the env repo can change the cluster. Protect the env repo with CODEOWNERS, required reviews, branch protection.
- **Rollback to an earlier commit causes CRD version mismatches** if CRDs were upgraded between revisions. Always plan CRD lifecycle separately from app manifests.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **GitOps = Git is desired state; a cluster controller reconciles** — pull-based, continuous drift reconciliation, audit via `git log`.
- **Rollback = `git revert`** — no special tooling; the controller applies the reverted state.
- **Pull-based security** — CI doesn't need cluster credentials; the cluster pulls from Git; huge win in regulated environments.
- **ArgoCD: Application/ApplicationSet CRDs, strong UI, multi-cluster from management cluster** — opinionated and UX-rich.
- **Flux: modular controllers, native Helm releases, first-class image automation** — Kubernetes-native building blocks.
- **Secrets need vault or encryption** — External Secrets Operator, Sealed Secrets, or SOPS; never plain.
- **Progressive delivery layers on top** — Argo Rollouts (ArgoCD) or Flagger (Flux) for canary with automated analysis.
- **Auto-sync + prune is powerful but risky** — require protected branches, PR review, and selective prune scope.
- **RBAC on the env Git repo is the real access control** — anyone who merges can change the cluster; CODEOWNERS + required reviews matter.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
GitOps is a deployment model where Git is the single source of truth for the cluster's desired state, and a controller running inside the cluster continuously reconciles that state by pulling from Git.

**Core properties**
- Deployment is declarative: you commit YAML or Helm/Kustomize to Git; the controller applies it.
- Rollback is `git revert`; audit is `git log`; drift detection is continuous because the controller keeps reconciling.
- Pull-based security: the cluster pulls from Git; CI never needs cluster credentials, which is a big win for regulated environments.

**ArgoCD**
- Opinionated with a strong UI. An Application CRD points at a Git path + destination cluster/namespace with a sync policy.
- ApplicationSet templates many Applications — add an environment, an Application appears.
- Multi-cluster from a management cluster; strong RBAC via Projects; progressive delivery via Argo Rollouts.
- Helm gotcha — renders with `helm template` by default, so `helm history` is empty; rollback is Git revert.

**Flux**
- Modular set of controllers: source-controller, kustomize-controller, helm-controller, notification-controller, image-automation-controller.
- HelmRelease creates REAL Helm releases so `helm history` and `helm rollback` work natively.
- Image automation watches registries and commits new tags back to Git automatically — closes the loop without a separate CI bump job.
- Lightweight, per-cluster deployment; UI story is weaker out of the box (use Weave GitOps or Flux UI add-ons).

**Secrets**
- Never commit plain secrets. Three options: Sealed Secrets (encrypt to cluster public key), SOPS (KMS-encrypted YAML; Flux has native support), External Secrets Operator (sync from AWS Secrets Manager / Vault / Azure Key Vault).
- ESO is the modern default — secrets stay in a purpose-built vault, ESO syncs on demand, rotation handled by the vault.

**Progressive delivery**
- Argo Rollouts replaces Deployment with a canary or blue-green spec that runs automated analysis (Prometheus queries) before promoting.
- Flagger does similar canary work integrating with service mesh traffic weighting; works with plain Deployments.

**Decision guidance**
- Pick ArgoCD for UI-driven multi-team visibility and multi-cluster fan-out from a central control plane.
- Pick Flux for native Helm release support, image automation, and a Kubernetes-native building-block approach.
- Both are CNCF graduated and production-grade.

**Common gotchas**
- Auto-sync plus prune in prod without branch protection is dangerous — require PR review and CODEOWNERS.
- Operator-managed CR fields drift (e.g., status) — mark them as IgnoreDifferences.
- Large repos slow reconciliation — split sources or scope Applications by path.
- RBAC on the env Git repo IS the access control — anyone who merges can change the cluster.

speakable_v2.hook: GitOps is a deployment model where Git is the single source of truth for the cluster's desired state, and a controller running inside the cluster continuously reconciles that state by pulling from Git.

beats.text: Before GitOps, deployment was imperative: a CI job ran kubectl apply (or helm upgrade) against the cluster from outside. The cluster had no memory of desired state beyond what was last applied. Drift — when live state diverges from what was intended — went unnoticed.

items: GitOps = Git is desired state; a cluster controller reconciles — pull-based, continuous drift reconciliation, audit via git log
Rollback = git revert — no special tooling; the controller applies the reverted state
Pull-based security — CI doesn't need cluster credentials; the cluster pulls from Git; huge win in regulated environments
ArgoCD: Application/ApplicationSet CRDs, strong UI, multi-cluster from management cluster — opinionated and UX-rich
Flux: modular controllers, native Helm releases, first-class image automation — Kubernetes-native building blocks
Secrets in GitOps
Plain secrets in Git is a no-go
Three mainstream patterns: Sealed Secrets (Bitnami)
Encrypt secrets into SealedSecret CR using cluster's public key; kubeseal CLI encrypts
Sealed Secret controller decrypts inside cluster
